I pronoun

also me, it’s me, with me

classical

Ter. And. 348: Obtundis, tametsī intellegō.
Cic. Att. 5.1.3: tū invītā mulierēs, ego virōs accīverō

ego, meī

pronoun, first person: dative mihi, accusative and ablative mē; plural nōs · Wiktionary

I, me

Latin leaves the subject out: the ending of the verb already says “I” (intellegō). Ego is said only for stress or contrast, as in “you invite the women, I’ll fetch the men”; a needless ego at every turn is English underneath. “It’s me” is Ego sum. “With me” is mēcum, the preposition put after the pronoun.

Other words

  • egomet — I myself, I for my part

    pronoun: ego with the suffix -met · also used · classical · Plaut. Am. 2.1.60: Quis tē verberāvit? — Egomet mēmet. (Lewis & Short, s.v. ego) · Wiktionary

    A stronger ego; the suffix -met also strengthens the other cases (mēmet, mihimet, nōsmet).

Examples

  • Obtundis, tametsī intellegō.

    You keep on at me, though I understand.Ter. And. 348

  • Pompōnia, inquit, tū invītā mulierēs, ego virōs accīverō

    “Pomponia,” he said, “you invite the women, and I’ll have fetched the men.”Cic. Att. 5.1.3

  • sī valēs, bene est; ego valeō

    If you are well, good; I am well.Plin. Ep. 1.11.1

  • Num tū intellegis hīc quid narret? — Num tū? — Nihil. — Tantundem ego.

    Do you understand what he’s saying? — Do you? — Not a thing. — No more do I.Ter. Ph. 846

  • heus, ecquis hīc est? ecquis hoc aperit ōstium? — Quis ad forēs est? — Ego sum.

    Hey, is anyone there? Will anyone open this door? — Who’s at the door? — It’s me.Plaut. Amph. 1020–1021b

  • salvē, inquit illa; cūr mē fūgistī, obsecrō?

    “Hello,” she said; “why did you run away from me, please?”Phaedr. App. 32.5

  • ōlim mihi nūllās epistulās mittis

    For a long time now you’ve sent me no letters.Plin. Ep. 1.11.1

  • venī ergō mēcum

    Come with me, then.Phaedr. 3.7.15
